https://www.dw.com/en/can-a-massive-mado.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IpP1 People have been coming to see the statue of the Virgin Mary in Konotopie even before it is officially opened to the public on Saturday Image: Mateusz Kaczmarek/REUTERS Advertisement With its grain fields, meadows and lake, the countryside around the tiny village of Konotopie in central Poland is idyllic. Towering above all this is a monumental statue of the Virgin Mary. Home to just 120 residents and situated about 160 kilometers (99 miles) northwest of the capital, Warsaw, the previously little-known village of Konotopie has been in the headlines for weeks now as a result of the massive statue. The snow-white structure, which is visible for miles around, is over 55 meters (180 feet) tall. The statue itself is 40.6 meters high and stands on a 15-meter-high pedestal shaped like a crown that is intended to serve as a viewing platform. The figure dwarfs Rio de Janeiro's famous statue of Christ the Redeemer, which reaches a total height of 38 meters including its base. A 'pile of concrete' or a 'fantastic achievement'? The statue will be officially inaugurated on Saturday, August 15, the feast of the Assumption of Mary, a major holy day in the Catholic calendar. Although final construction work is still underway and the site remains fenced off and guarded, thousands of people — both pilgrims and sightseers — have been flocking to see it for months. Opinion about the project is divided. "It's a nightmare," one critic of the statue told the weekly magazine Newsweek, "a complete waste. Instead of investing that money in useful projects, they financed a giant pile of concrete." "This Mary is absolutely beautiful. My utmost respect. A fantastic achievement," said one devout lady visiting the site, according to the right-wing conservative weekly Sieci . Wealthy, devout benefactor The benefactor behind the statue, 75-year-old Roman Karkosik, hails from a nearby village and is one of Poland's wealthiest individuals. Nearly 40 years ago, when the shortage economy of socialism gave way to free-market capitalism after the collapse of communism in eastern Europe, Karkosik was a young graduate from technical high school. He started out as a bartender, but moved on to buying and selling scrap metal, producing soft drinks and later became the first entrepreneur in Poland to manufacture plastic bottles. The inauguration ceremony for the Marian statue coincides with a major Catholic holy day, the Feast of the Assumption of Mary, on August 15 Image: Kuba Stezycki/REUTERS Karkosik made a name for himself on the Warsaw Stock Exchange. Some journalists have compared his role in Poland to Warren Buffett's influence on Wall Street. His fortune is estimated at roughly €442 million ($511 million), and he ranks 44th on Wprost magazine's list of Poland's richest people. He lives in an 18th-century manor in the town of Kikol, just two kilometers from Konotopie. A 'gesture of gratitude' Karkosik and his wife, Grazyna, avoid both public appearances and contact with the media. The cost of the statue remains a closely guarded secret. Media reports speculate that the project may have cost as much as €23 million. The Karkosiks have described the Marian statue as a "gesture of gratitude." According to media reports, the devout businessman wanted to thank the Virgin Mary for his recovery from a serious illness. His two brothers, who were also successful businessmen, both died prematurely after illnesses. This is not the first time Karkosik has provided money for a religious structure. Back in 2011, he funded the construction of a church at a nearby pilgrimage site. Artist feared seeing the finished statue "I was afraid to come to Konotopie to see what had become of my design in reality," sculptor Adam Jakub Matejkowski told Polish media. Worried that the hands and face of the Virgin Mary might appear distorted, Matejkowski only visited the site in July. "I opened my eyes and was stunned. The Mother of God is opening her arms to embrace us," he said with satisfaction. "That was exactly my intention: for the figure to have a human character, to come toward us," he explained. The statue of Jesus Christ the King of the Universe in Swiebodzin, one of the tallest Jesus statues in the world, is also in Poland Image: Monika Skolimowska/ZB/dpa/picture alliance Matejkowski says the statue has the facial expression of his 11-year-old daughter and the delicate facial features of his wife. Region hopes for economic boost Konotopie is situated in one of Poland's economically weak regions. There are no major industrial employers here, and jobs are scarce. Local leaders hope the Marian statue will stimulate economic growth. "The monument is not only a spiritual landmark but also a strategic asset for the region. We expect it to attract more investors and tourists, which will benefit the local economy," Krzysztof Kowalewski of the authorities in the nearby town of Kikol told Polish media. Mayor Renata Golebiewska has said that revenues at local restaurants and bars have already broken local records. Not the first statue of its kind in Poland Poland is well known for its monumental Christian structures. Following Poland's transition to democracy in 1989, a massive basilica was built in the village of Lichen in central Poland, overshadowing even the cathedrals of Paris and Cologne in scale. The basilica is 138 meters (453 feet) long, 77 meters wide, and features a dome with a diameter of 35 meters. It can accommodate 20,000 worshippers. Since 2010, Poland has also been home to the world's tallest statue of Jesus. Located in Swiebodzin near the German border, the 36-meter-high statue stands on a 17-meter-high mound. Rising secularization Whether all these gigantic monuments can stop the ongoing secularization of Polish society, however, remains highly questionable. Although Poland is still one of the most Catholic countries in Europe, public trust in the Church continues to decline . For centuries, the Catholic faith was a key part of Polish identity. A huge statue of Pope John Paul II, who was born in Poland and was head of the Catholic Church from 1978 to 2005, in Czestochowa Image: Waldemar Deska/dpa/picture alliance In the 19th century, when the territory that now makes up Poland was not an independent state and was divided up among foreign powers, Catholicism played a major role in the resistance to Protestant Prussia and Orthodox Russia. After World War II, despite ideological differences, the anti-communist opposition and the Catholic Church in Poland worked together against the communist dictatorship. During this period, churches became refuges for persecuted dissidents, and several priests were murdered by the secret police. Pope John Paul II , himself Polish, also played a significant role in the struggle against the regime. Catholicism in modern-day Poland Since Poland's transition to democracy in 1989, however, the Catholic Church has experienced a crisis similar to that seen across Europe. According to a September 2025 survey conducted by the Polish polling institute IBRIS, only 35% of Poles still trust the Church, down from 58% in 2016. Distrust rose from 24% to 47% over the same period. In 2026, the annual number of priests ordained in Poland fell below 200 for the first time since 2000. Church attendance has also been steadily declining, especially among young people. Even a gigantic Madonna is unlikely to reverse that trend. This article was originally published in German. https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/08/17/w.text: BUDAPEST — A passenger bus traveling on a highway in Hungary early Sunday went off the road and into a ditch where it overturned, killing 12 and injuring others, police said.The bus, which carried Polish license plates, was traveling on eastbound lanes near the town of Mezokeresztes when it overturned on the M3 motorway around 140 kilometers east of Hungary’s capital, Budapest, at around 1 a.m. on Sunday.In a statement, police said it was likely that the driver fell asleep, causing the accident, and that the driver had been taken into custody.Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski wrote Sunday in a post on X that a “tragic bus accident involving Polish tourists” had occurred in Hungary and that his ministry was in contact with Hungarian authorities.Polish President Karol Nawrocki expressed his “deep sorrow” over the accident.“I join the families and loved ones of the victims in prayer and deep sympathy,” he wrote in a post on X.Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar wrote in a statement on Facebook that at least 10 people were seriously injured in the crash. He offered his condolences to the families of the victims and thanked rescue workers who were dispatched to the scene.

Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty Images Ethical foreign policy UK sanctions on Israel ‘fall far short’ of its obligations, legal experts say More than 130 sign letter to PM saying international law requires further measures to stop illegal settlements Haroon Siddique and Geneva Abdul Tue 15 Sep 2026 07.54 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 10.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More than 130 legal experts, including 18 king’s counsel (KCs), have written to Andy Burnham saying that sanctions on Israeli settlements “fall far short” of Britain’s obligations under the international court of justice’s (ICJ’s) finding that the occupation is unlawful. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, last week announced an import ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in Palestine and other measures. Signatories to the letter to the prime minister, including the leading lawyers Michael Mansfield KC and Imran Khan KC, and the former lord justice of appeal Alan Moses, say it is not enough. In a 2024 advisory opinion, the ICJ, which is the UN’s top court, ordered Israel to end the occupation “as rapidly as possible” and said other countries were under an obligation not to recognise the occupation as lawful nor aid or assist it. The letter, sent on Tuesday, says the ICJ’s findings have “not had an impact on Israel’s apartheid practice” and, while the UK sanctions are “a necessary corrective”, they are “improperly narrow” when compared with sanctions on Russia, which are not limited to economic activity in occupied Ukrainian territory but apply to wider economic structures supporting the unlawful conduct. It says: “We ask it to commit to further and more rigorous measures to ensure that no part of the UK’s economic relationship with Israel continues to sustain the illegal occupation itself, and the settlements and other serious violations of fundamental rules of international law perpetrated through its conduct, and to build on this to adopt robust coercive measures to seek to bring all these serious violations of international law, and the practices they sustain, including, fundamentally, the occupation itself, to an end. The letter, also signed by legal academics, calls for a range of additional measures including a full arms embargo on Israel. When announcing the sanctions, Miliband accused Israel of ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, and the signatories say article 6(3) of the arms trade treaty prohibits transfers of arms where a state has knowledge of such a crime. The sanctions were announced after escalating attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinian villages in the West Bank and an Israeli tender was issued for 1,200 homes in the E1 settlement , east of Jerusalem, which could in effect cut off the north from the south of the West Bank, threatening the viability of any future Palestinian state. The signatories want extension of the sanctions to cover insurance, accountancy services and digital infrastructure as well as public confirmation that no UK public body, pension scheme or sovereign fund holds settlement investments. One of the letter’s signatories and drafters, Ralph Wilde, a professor of international law at University College London, welcomed the UK’s recent recognition of Israel’s occupation of the West Bank as unlawful as an “important shift”, but said it fell short in its focus on the settlements and settlers. “The elephant in the room is the illegality of the occupation itself,” said Wilde, who acted as senior counsel and legal adviser to the Arab League in the case before the ICJ. “It’s not just simply the settlements and the abuse of treatment and the genocide, which of course are also wrong, it’s Israel’s very presence.” He added: “There’s a mismatch between saying Israel’s very presence there is illegal, but then only focusing on the question of the settlers and the settlements. If the problem is with the settlements themselves, then the problem is with the state that establishes them.” A government spokesperson said: “This is the biggest reset in the UK’s approach to protecting and securing the two-state solution in a generation. We have shown our commitment to international law and our refusal to be bystanders to further suffering. “We have taken concrete action, supported accountability, pledged to galvanise the international community and acted with our partners across the globe.” In response to the sanctions, the Israeli foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, accused Miliband of “outrageous lies” and said the UK government was “systematically working against the state of Israel”. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/16/yeme.text: Yemen's Houthis on Wednesday said they shot down a Saudi fighter jet, claiming they used munitions made by the group to target the warplane."The Yemeni Armed Forces, with Allah's aid and grace, succeeded in shooting down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet while it was carrying out hostile operations," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on social media, while accusing Saudi Arabia of launching 450 strikes.He said the aircraft had been targeted "using a locally made air-to-air missile".The spokesman also dismissed Saudi claims that the Houthis had targeted Islam's holy city of Mecca."Our operations target its oil facilities and military bases, which are far removed from the sacred sites," he said, adding that "fabrications and lies propagated by the criminal al-Saud regime cannot deceive anyone."The Saudi coalition vowed retaliation, warning that the security of holy sites was a "red line"."The security of the Two Holy Mosques and the pilgrims is a red line, and the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the terrorist Houthi militia," the coalition said in a statement shared by spokesman Turki al-Maliki on X.Saudi Arabia had issued brief alerts on Tuesday over possible attacks in Mecca and across swathes of the kingdom's south, which borders Yemen.The alerts, including the first one issued in Mecca since the Iran war erupted in February, came a day after a wave of ballistic missile and drone attacks launched from Yemen wounded 13 people in the kingdom's south.Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned on Wednesday "in the strongest possible terms the dastardly and heinous" attack on Mecca."The people of Pakistan are saddened and perturbed by this outrageous act," he said on X.The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, a 57-member bloc of Muslim-majority countries, also condemned the "heinous" attack.The Houthis are Zaydi Shia Muslims, a specific branch of Islam historically rooted in northern Yemen that is theologically distinct from both the Twelver Shia Islam dominant in Iran and Saudi Arabia's Wahhabi-influenced Sunni tradition.Mecca is Islam's holiest site, home to the Kaaba — which Muslims worldwide turn toward for prayer — and the destination of the Hajj pilgrimage, one of the faith's Five Pillars or main tenets.Any confirmed attack on the city would put the perpetrators beyond the pale in the eyes of virtually the entire Muslim world, Shia and Sunni alike.Warnings over Bab el-Mandeb spikeFormally known as Ansar Allah, the Houthis have been engaged in renewed fighting with the internationally recognised government forces since Yemen's civil war reignited in July.The fighting in the Arabian Peninsula's poorest country has forced 82,000 people to flee their homes since the start of September, according to the UN.Yemen's permanent representative at the UN Abdullah al-Saadi said his compatriots were fighting to restore "national institutions across every inch of their land", and called on the international community to take action against the Houthis.The group has also declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and has been targeting its ships in the Red Sea.In a lightning offensive last week, the Houthis seized control of the entirety of Yemen's Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb strait.One of the world's crucial waterways connecting the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and the main chokehold on the cargo route to the Mediterranean and Europe has become vital to Saudi crude exports as the wider Middle East war chokes the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.The Houthis have insisted that there is no threat to navigation in the Bab el-Mandeb except for Saudi vessels.Any attacks in the waterway are likely to make it less attractive to shippers.Disruption in the strait could also endanger Egypt, as the Red Sea serves as the gateway to the Suez Canal, on which Cairo relies for crucial foreign revenue.Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi called on Tuesday for "ensuring the freedom and security of maritime navigation" through the Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, the Egyptian presidency said.On Tuesday, Qatar warned of dire consequences if Bab el-Mandeb was closed, saying it would be "catastrophic for the entire world".US media reported last week that the Saudi crown prince made a personal request to President Donald Trump for US intervention, but it was turned down. Neither Riyadh nor Washington have issued any statements regarding these reports.However, a US military task force is working to enhance intelligence-sharing and planning assistance for Saudi forces as they face attacks, a US official told AFP on Tuesday.Canal revenues are currently around half of what they were before the Houthis first started attacking Red Sea shipping in 2023, a campaign they said was in solidarity with Palestinians during the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza.The Houthis have also targeted oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, the world's leading crude exporter, pushing global prices above the $100-a-barrel threshold.The Saudi-led coalition said it would deal with the attacks "firmly to protect the sovereignty of the Kingdom", and would take "all necessary operational measures to deter this ... hostile and extremist approach".The Houthis are tied to Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.

https://hotnews.ro/taxa-pe-avere-care-i-.text: Proiecțiile realizate de mass-media din SUA la aproape o săptămână de la scrutin arată că alegătorii din California au respins prin referendum propunerea de taxare a averilor miliardarilor din acest stat, o măsură controversată care a stârnit o opoziție puternică în Silicon Valley, transmite marți agenția AFP, citată de Agerpres . Numărarea voturilor nu fusese încă finalizată marți, însă principalele rețele americane de televiziune au anunțat că problema a fost tranșată: „Propunerea 40” nu a reușit să obțină sprijinul majorității votanților, potrivit proiecțiilor CNN și CBS News . Potrivit cotidianului Los Angeles Times , propunea a fost respinsă în marea majoritate a comitatelor, dar a primit sprijinul alegătorilor din marile orașe Los Angeles și San Francisco. Referendumul s-a desfășurat în data de 3 noiembrie, simultan cu alegerile de la jumătatea mandatului pentru Congres și alegerea guvernatorilor în mai multe state americane. Deși populară la lansare, propunerea de taxare a părut rapid sortită eșecului la urne, în ciuda votului semnificativ de stânga și a victoriei democraților la alegerile de la jumătatea mandatului. A doua zi după referendum, votul „nu” conducea cu un scor de peste 55% după numărarea a aproximativ 60% dintre buletine. Inițiativa propunea taxarea celor aproximativ 200 de miliardari din California cu 5% din averea lor netă pentru a finanța sistemul public de sănătate, de care depind jumătate dintre californieni, un sistem slăbit de reducerile federale masive impuse de președintele Donald Trump. Taxa urma să fie aplicată o singură dată, iar susținătorii săi sperau să se strângă astfel aproximativ 100 de miliarde de dolari. California, centrul industriei tehnologice din SUA, este cel mai populat stat american și ar fi a patra cea mai mare economie a lumii dacă ar fi o țară, însă decalajul dintre bogați și săraci este foarte mare. Oponenții „Propunerii 40”, printre care Mark Zuckerberg și cofondatorul Google Sergey Brin, au cheltuit sute de milioane de dolari pe publicitate la televiziune înaintea votului, susținând că taxa riscă să devină permanentă și să declanșeze un exod al ultra-bogaților și o scădere a veniturilor fiscale. Propunerea a stârnit un val de reacții negative din partea oamenilor de afaceri din California, fondatorii startup-urilor și companiilor din domeniul tehnologiei plângându-se cu predilecție că vor fi afectați în mod disproporționat. Asta fiindcă ei ar urma să fie taxați în baza evaluării companiilor lor, care e adesea de sute de ori mai mare decât numerarul sau celelalte active mai lichide pe care le dețin. În esență, miliardarii tech spun că, dacă propunerea de taxă va fi aprobată, ei vor fi nevoiți să vândă pachete de acțiuni din companiile lor pentru a putea plăti suma ce le va fi impusă. Gavin Newsom, guvernatorul la final de mandat al Californiei și un potențial candidat la nominalizarea Partidului Democrat pentru alegerile prezidențiale din 2028, s-a opus și el acestei taxe. Mai multe tentative de impozitare a marilor averi au eșuat anterior în California, fără a ajunge niciodată la urne. HotNews.ro utilizează cookie-uri pentru a îmbunătăți experiența dvs . Photograph: David Swanson/AP Los Angeles Three dead in Los Angeles after driver crashes into pedestrians, officials say Three others critically injured and taken to hospitals as reports say car crashed into food stand in North Hollywood Uwa Ede-Osifo Tue 10 Nov 2026 22.52 EST First published on Tue 10 Nov 2026 22.10 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google At least three people are dead and three critically injured, after a car struck pedestrians on a Los Angeles corner during Tuesday rush hour, authorities said. The fatal crash took place near a North Hollywood metro station. The driver, whose identity remains unknown, is hospitalized in critical condition, according to Los Angeles police. The three injured people ⁠were also taken to area hospitals for treatment, ​according to an ‌online statement posted ‌by the the LA fire department. The fire and police departments did not offer additional details on the deadly crash. A local CBS News affiliate station reported that the ‌car crashed into a food stand near a bus stop along a major ​thoroughfare, Lankershim Boulevard, that runs through the busy NoHo commercial and arts district in the city’s San Fernando Valley. Aerial news video footage of ⁠the scene showed a white-colored, partially crumpled ​small ​SUV that appeared ​to have run up onto the sidewalk and ​into the side of a mass-transit shelter structure. An investigation remains under way.
